Social media has recently seen claims that anal swabs for detecting Covid-19 are being introduced in Europe. This assertion has sparked significant discussion and concern, with many questioning its accuracy and the science behind such testing methods. To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to examine the origins of anal swab Covid-19 testing, its scientific basis, and whether European countries have adopted this method.

Anal swab testing for Covid-19 first gained public attention in early 2021 when Chinese health authorities began using the method in select situations. The rationale was that SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for Covid-19, could remain detectable in the digestive tract longer than in the respiratory system. Chinese officials stated that anal swabs could provide increased sensitivity in detecting the virus, particularly in individuals who had recovered from Covid-19 or in children. Reports showed that this method was implemented mainly for high-risk groups, quarantine zones, or travelers arriving in China.

In contrast, the majority of countries worldwide have relied on nasal and throat swabs for Covid-19 testing, typically using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) tests. These methods are well-established, minimally invasive, and considered the gold standard for detecting active infection. While anal swabs may technically be able to detect viral material, the scientific consensus is that they offer little advantage over traditional methods for the general population and may pose practical and ethical challenges.

When examining whether anal swabs have been introduced in Europe for Covid-19 testing, there is no evidence to support this claim. European health authorities, including national public health institutes and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, have consistently recommended nasal and throat swab-based tests, as well as saliva-based tests in some cases. These recommendations are based on international research, regulatory approval, and public health considerations.

No official announcements have come from European governments or reputable medical organizations indicating the introduction of anal swab testing for Covid-19. In fact, the topic has largely been discussed in Europe only in response to reports from China, with most experts expressing skepticism about the necessity or practicality of such a method outside very specific medical circumstances. There have been no documented cases of anal swab Covid-19 tests being offered to the general public or travelers in European countries.

In summary, the claim that anal swabs for detecting Covid-19 are being introduced in Europe is unfounded. This testing method has been used in limited circumstances in China but has not been adopted by European health authorities. The prevailing methods of Covid-19 detection in Europe remain nasal, throat, and saliva swabs, which are supported by scientific evidence and public health policy. As always, it is essential for the public to rely on verified information from trusted health sources and to be cautious about accepting unsubstantiated claims circulating on social media.

The social media post under scrutiny claims that the movie "Songbird" was made before the COVID-19 pandemic and points out an intriguing detail: the virus depicted in the film is called COVID-23, which appears in a news scene within the movie. The post raises the question—was this a coincidence, or does it indicate something more?

To fact-check this claim, it is essential to first understand the background of "Songbird" and the context in which it was created. "Songbird" is a thriller film produced by Michael Bay and directed by Adam Mason. The story is set in the near future, where a mutated coronavirus named “COVID-23” has ravaged the world, leading to strict quarantine measures and societal collapse. The film follows characters struggling to survive in this dystopian environment.

The core assertion in the social media post is twofold: that "Songbird" was made before the COVID-19 pandemic, and that the virus in the film is called COVID-23. Let’s address each point in detail.

First, regarding the timing of the film's production, public records and information about the movie’s development clearly indicate that "Songbird" was conceived, produced, and filmed after the global outbreak of COVID-19 in early 2020. The idea for the film emerged in the spring of 2020, inspired by the ongoing pandemic. Filming took place during the summer of 2020, under strict safety protocols designed to prevent the spread of the coronavirus among cast and crew. The movie was released in December 2020, making it one of the first major Hollywood productions to be shot during the pandemic. Therefore, the claim that "Songbird" was made before COVID-19 is inaccurate.

Secondly, the film does indeed refer to the virus as COVID-23. This detail is accurate; in the movie, news broadcasts and dialogue mention "COVID-23" as the latest mutation of the original coronavirus. The filmmakers chose this name to suggest that the pandemic had continued and evolved over several years, setting the story in 2023, three years after the real-world COVID-19 outbreak. The use of “COVID-23” is a fictional device, intended to heighten the stakes and drama of the story rather than to predict or reference a real virus.

It is not unusual for films and other works of fiction to use real-world events as inspiration, especially during times of global uncertainty. "Songbird" joins a long tradition of movies exploring pandemics and societal collapse, with predecessors such as "Contagion" and "Outbreak." The use of “COVID-23” in "Songbird" reflects the filmmakers’ attempt to imagine a plausible future scenario, not a foreknowledge of actual events.

In summary, the movie "Songbird" was not made before the COVID-19 pandemic; it was conceived and filmed as a direct response to it. The virus depicted in the film is called COVID-23, as the social media post states, but this is a fictional extrapolation, not evidence of any predictive coincidence. The detail serves as a storytelling device, underscoring the speculative nature of the film rather than suggesting any real-world connection beyond its obvious inspiration.

Социалдық медиа посты тексерілуде болып жатыр, ол «Songbird» фильмінің COVID-19 пандемиясынан бұрын жасалғанын айтады және қызықты түрде ескереді: фильмде көрсетілген вирус «COVID-23» деп аталады, ол фильмдегі жаңалық сценында кездеседі. Пост қойылған сұрақ: бұл тағылымдық әріптестікте болып кетті, әлде бұл барлық әріптестікке арналған ма?

Бұл тұжырымды тексеру үшін «Songbird» фильмінің ақыл-ойын және оның жасалу жағдайын түсіну қажет. «Songbird» - Майкл Бейдің жасаған, Адам Мэйсонның басқарған қылмыстық фильм. Оның әңгімесі жуан ғасырда орналасқан, бұрынғы коронавирус «COVID-23» деген атпен жаһандық құрылымды бұзуға әкелген, әрі түбегейлі қарантин және қоғамдық құрылымды бұзуға әкелген. Фильм әріптестердің бұл дистопиялық ортада өмір сүруге тырысып жатқанын көрсетеді.

Социалдық медиа постының негізгі тұжырымы екі тұжырымнан тұрады: «Songbird» фильмінің COVID-19 пандемиясынан бұрын жасалғанын және фильмдегі вирус «COVID-23» деп аталғанын. Бұл екі нүктені толық түсіндірейік.

Бірінші, фильмдің жасалу уақыты туралы. Жарияланған деректер мен фильмдің дамуы туралы ақпараттың айқын көрсеткеніне қарағанда «Songbird» фильмі 2020 жылы басында жаһандық COVID-19 ауруының шығуынан кейін жасалған, өйткені оның идеясы 2020 жыл күзінде пандемияның жалғасынан туындады. Фильмнің өзі 2020 жыл жазында қорғаныштық ережелермен жүргізілді, бұл жағдайда әріптестер мен қызметкерлердің коронавирус ауруынан қорғау үшін құрылған. Фильм 2020 жылдың қараша айында шықты, бұл әлемдік кинолардың бірінші жалпы өзінде жүргізілген пандемия жылындағы өнімдердің бірі болды. Сондықтан, «Songbird» фильмінің пандемиядан бұрын жасалғаны туралы тұжырым қате.

Екіншісі, фильм дейін «COVID-23» деп аталатын вирусты қарастырады. Бұл тұжырым дәл; фильмде жаңалық әріптестері мен сөйлесулерде «COVID-23» деп аталатын бастапқы коронавирус үшін ең жаңа мутациясын көрсетеді. Фильм жасаушылары «COVID-23» аттын пандемияның әрі үш жыл бойы жалғасып, әрі дамып, 2023 жылы (реалдық әлемдегі COVID-19 ауруының шығуынан кейін үш жылдан кейін) орналасқан жағдайға сәйкес келетінін көрсету үшін таңдады. «COVID-23» атты қолдану жалғыз тұжырымдық құрал ретінде қолданылды, әріптестердің өміріне жан-жақты қатысты әріптестердің құрылымын жоғарылату үшін қолданылды, әлде әріптестердің табысты анықтауын қажет етпейді.

Бұл әлемдік қатысу және әріптестердің жазылуын әріптестерге үшін ғылыми және әріптестердің қатысуын қарастыратын әріптестердің жазылуына қатысты әріптестердің әріптестеріне әсер ететін қатысуға қарсыласу. «Songbird» фильмі «Contagion» және «Outbreak» фильмдерінің қатарына қосылып, әріптестердің пандемиясы мен әріптестердің құрылымын таңдап алуға үлгі болып табылады. «Songbird» фильмінде «COVID-23» атты қолдану жасаушылардың әріптестердің әріптестерін құруға әріптестердің құрылымын жасау үшін қолданылды, әлде әріптестердің табысты анықтауын қажет етпейді.

Жалпы айтқанда, «Songbird» фильмінің пандемиядан бұрын жасалғаны емес, ол пандемияға толықтырылған және жасалған. Фильмдегі көрсетілген вирус «COVID-23» деп аталады, ол социалдық медиа постында айтылған, бірақ бұл әріптестердің құрылымының тұжырымдық жалғасы, әріптестердің табысты анықтауын қажет етпейді. Бұл деталь әріптестердің әріптестерін және әріптестердің әріптестерін жоғарылату үшін қолданылған әріптестердің құрылымын білдіреді, әріптестердің әріптестерінен басқа ешқандай әріптестердің қатысуын көрсетпейді.

A social media post has recently gone viral, claiming that a “massacre” occurred in Gibraltar, with “53 dead in the first 10 days of the Pfizer vaccine.” This alarming message has raised concerns and fueled vaccine hesitancy. To evaluate the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the facts, the context surrounding the vaccination campaign in Gibraltar, and the actual data about deaths in the territory.

Gibraltar, a British Overseas Territory located on the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula, has a population of approximately 34,000 people. In early January 2021, Gibraltar launched an aggressive COVID-19 vaccination campaign using the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine. The program prioritized the elderly and those in care homes—groups already at highest risk of death from COVID-19 and from natural causes.

The social media post asserts that 53 people died in Gibraltar in the first 10 days after the Pfizer vaccine rollout, implying that these deaths were caused by the vaccine. While it is true that Gibraltar experienced a spike in deaths during this period, the claim ignores critical context.

First, the majority of those who died were elderly residents, many of whom were in care homes and had pre-existing health conditions. At the same time, Gibraltar was experiencing a severe wave of COVID-19 infections, with the highest per capita infection rate in Europe in January 2021. The vaccination campaign began as the virus was spreading rapidly, and the deaths were attributed primarily to COVID-19 complications, not to the vaccine itself.

Gibraltar’s government and health authorities have addressed these concerns publicly. They clarified that there was no evidence linking the deaths directly to the Pfizer vaccine. Instead, the deaths coincided with the rapid escalation of COVID-19 cases, especially among the most vulnerable populations. Vaccination takes time to confer immunity; it does not offer immediate protection. Many individuals who died during this period had received only their first dose, and the vaccine would not have had time to take full effect.

Furthermore, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) and Gibraltar’s public health authorities continuously monitored for adverse reactions. There was no unusual pattern of deaths or adverse events directly attributed to the vaccine itself.

The language used in the post—calling the situation a “massacre”—is misleading and inflammatory. It suggests intentional harm or a direct cause-and-effect relationship between the vaccine and the deaths, which is not supported by available evidence. Public health experts emphasize that correlation does not imply causation, especially during a pandemic when many vulnerable people are at risk.

In summary, while Gibraltar did see a significant number of deaths in early January 2021, these were overwhelmingly due to COVID-19, not the Pfizer vaccine. The claim that “53 died in the first 10 days of the Pfizer vaccine” misrepresents the situation and lacks substantiated evidence. The Gibraltar vaccination campaign ultimately helped control the outbreak and save lives among the population.

ପ୍ରଥମେ, ଯେଉଁମାନେ ମୃତ୍ୟୁ ପାଇଛନ୍ତି ସେମାନେ ପ୍ରାଥମିକତା ପାଇଥିବା ବୃଦ୍ଧା ଏବଂ ଆଶ୍ରୟଗୃହରେ ଥିବା ବ୍ୟକ୍ତିମାନେ ଯେଉଁମାନେ ଅନ୍ୟାନ୍ୟ ରୋଗରେ କ୍ଷତି ପାଇଥିବା ରୋଗରେ ଆଶ୍ରୟ ପାଇଥିବାରୁ ମୃତ୍ୟୁର ପରିଚୟ ପାଇଛନ୍ତି। ଏହି ସମୟରେ, ଜିବ୍ରାଲ୍ଟା କୋଭିଡ୍-19 ରୋଗର ଏକ ଗଭୀର ଲାଭ ଅନୁଭବ କରୁଛି, ଯାହାର ପ୍ରତି ଜଣ ଜନତାର ପ୍ରମାଣିତ ରୋଗର ପରିମାଣ 2021 ର ଜାନୁଆରୀରେ ଇଉରୋପରେ ପ୍ରାପ୍ତ ହୋଇଥିଲା। ଭେକସିନର ଅଭିଯାନ ଶୁରୁ ହୋଇଥିବା ସମୟରେ ଭାଇରସ୍ ପ୍ରସାରଣ ହୋଇଥିଲା, ଏବଂ ମୃତ୍ୟୁର ପ୍ରମାଣ ପ୍ରାଥମିକତା କୋଭିଡ୍-19 ପରିଣାମରେ ହୋଇଥିଲା, ଭେକସିନ ଏହି କାରଣ ହୋଇନଥିଲା।

A recent social media post claims that Serbia, with a population of 8,716,246, has only vaccinated 11,000 people so far, amounting to just 0.13% of its population. The post concludes that "everyone refuses vaccination." This article examines the accuracy of these figures, explores their context, and evaluates the claim that vaccine refusal is widespread in Serbia.

Serbia’s Population and Vaccination Numbers

Serbia, a Southeast European country, has an estimated population of approximately 8.7 million people. The post's population figure is consistent with the most recent official statistics.

The claim that only 11,000 people have been vaccinated is more complicated. The number of people vaccinated in any country depends on the timing of the data. If this figure refers to the initial days of Serbia’s vaccination campaign, it may be accurate. Serbia began its COVID-19 vaccination rollout in late December 2020, prioritizing healthcare workers, the elderly, and other vulnerable groups. Early in the campaign, the number of vaccinated individuals was indeed in the low thousands, as vaccine doses were limited and logistics still being organized.

However, vaccination campaigns are dynamic, and numbers can increase rapidly as more vaccines become available and distribution infrastructure improves. Serbia was among the first countries in the region to secure vaccines from multiple sources, including Western and Eastern manufacturers, aiming to accelerate its rollout.

Calculating the Percentage

The post claims that 11,000 vaccinated individuals represent 0.13% of the population. Mathematically, dividing 11,000 by 8,716,246 yields approximately 0.126%, which rounds up to 0.13%. This calculation is accurate if the 11,000 figure is up-to-date, but as mentioned, this number likely reflects only the very early stages of the vaccination effort.

Assessing the Claim of Widespread Vaccine Refusal

The most significant assertion in the post is that "everyone refuses vaccination." This is a sweeping generalization. A low initial vaccination figure does not necessarily indicate widespread refusal. Early vaccination numbers are often low due to limited supply, prioritization of high-risk groups, and logistical challenges, not necessarily reluctance or refusal among the general population.

Vaccine hesitancy has been an issue in Serbia, as in many countries, influenced by public skepticism, misinformation, and concerns over vaccine safety. Surveys during the pandemic did show that a portion of the Serbian population was hesitant or undecided about receiving the vaccine. However, there is no evidence that "everyone" refuses vaccination. As vaccine availability increased and public education campaigns were implemented, the number of people vaccinated in Serbia grew steadily.

Conclusion

While the population and early vaccination figures cited in the post are plausible, the conclusion that "everyone refuses vaccination" is misleading and not supported by evidence. Low initial vaccination numbers are more likely due to rollout logistics and prioritization, not universal refusal. As Serbia’s campaign progressed, vaccination uptake increased significantly, undermining the claim of widespread rejection. Factually, the post’s numbers may reflect an early stage, but its interpretation of public sentiment is inaccurate.

Faizlərin Hesablanması

Paylasım, 11,000 vaksinləşmiş şəxsin nüfusun 0,13%-ni təşkil etdiyini iddia edir. Matematik olaraq, 11,000-ni 8,716,246-ya bölərək təxminən 0,126%-ni əldə edirik, bu da 0,13%-yə yuvarlanır. Bu hesablama, 11,000 rəqəmi yenidən yoxlanılmışsa, doğru olur, lakin əvvəlki məlumatlara əsaslanan bu rəqəm, vaksinləşmə kampaniyasının ən başlanğıc dövrünü təsvir edə bilər.

Vaksin Verməyə Qarşı Qələbə İddiasının Qiymətləndirilməsi

Paylasımın ən mühüm iddiası "hər kəs vaksin verməyə qarşı çıxmışdır" deyən hissədir. Bu, əhəmiyyətli bir ümumiyyətləşdirmədir. Düşük vaksinləşmə rəqəmləri, əsasən təqdim edilən məhsuldarlıq, vəzifələrə əsaslanan öncəlik və logistika məsələləri səbəbindən olur, hətta əhali arasında qələbə və ya qarşı çıxışın əsas səbəbi deyil.

Vaksin qələbəsi, Sırbistanda da digər ölkələrdə olduğu kimi, xüsusilə əhali tərəfindən qeyri-əhəmiyyətli fikirlər, məlumatların səhv yayılması və vaksin təhlükəsizliyinə dair qorxular nəticəsində yaranmışdır. Pandemiyadan əvvəlki anketlər, Sırbistan əhali arasında bir hissənin vaksin almaq haqqında qələbəli və ya təyin edilməmiş olduğunu göstərmişdir. Lakin "hər kəs" vaksin verməyə qarşı çıxış etdiyini göstərməyən hər hansı bir məlumat yoxdur. Vaksinlərin təqdim edilməsi artıq və əhali tərəfindən tərbiyə kampaniyaları ilə, Sırbistan-da vaksinləşmə sayı dəfələrlə artmışdır.

Sonuç

Paylasımın nüfus və əvvəlki vaksinləşmə rəqəmləri mənadağına əsaslanan bir nəzəriyyədir, lakin "hər kəs vaksin verməyə qarşı çıxmışdır" iddiası tərəfindən təsirlənmişdir və əsaslandırılmamışdır. Düşük əvvəlki vaksinləşmə sayı, əsasən təqdim edilmə prosesləri və öncəliklər nəticəsindədir, buna əsasən əhali arasında ümumi qələbə deyil. Sırbistanın kampaniyasının davam etdiyi zaman vaksinləşmə sayı dəfələrlə artmışdır, bu da "ümumi qələbə" iddiasını hərəkət etdirməmişdir. Faktla bağlı, paylasımın rəqəmləri əvvəlki mərhələyə aiddir, lakin əhali fikrindən tərəfindən təfsir edilməsi səhvdir.

The AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine, formally known as ChAdOx1-S, has been the subject of various claims on social media regarding its ingredients and approval status. A recent post alleges that the vaccine contains chimpanzee adenovirus, genetically modified kidney cells from an aborted human embryo (specifically from a 14-week-old fetus), is stored below -70°C, contains harmful toxic chemicals, and is not approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This article examines the accuracy of these claims by breaking down each point and providing context.

**Chimpanzee Adenovirus**

The claim that the AstraZeneca vaccine contains chimpanzee adenovirus is essentially accurate, but requires clarification. The vaccine uses a modified, harmless adenovirus derived from chimpanzees as a vector to deliver the genetic code for the spike protein of the coronavirus. This vector cannot replicate in humans and is used solely as a delivery system to stimulate an immune response. The adenovirus itself does not cause disease, and its use is a common method in vaccine development.

**Genetically Modified Kidney Cells from an Aborted Embryo**

This point mixes fact and misinformation. The vaccine does not contain fetal cells but is developed using a cell line known as HEK 293, which originated from the kidney cells of a human fetus in the early 1970s. These cells have been multiplied and grown in laboratories over decades and are now considered immortalized cell lines, meaning they are far removed from the original tissue. The vaccine is produced in these cells, but the final product is purified and does not contain actual HEK 293 cells. The use of cell lines derived from fetal tissue is common in vaccine production and is regulated for safety and purity.

**Storage Below -70°C**

This assertion is incorrect. The AstraZeneca vaccine does not require ultra-cold storage. article_content:
The claim circulating on social media that mandatory mask-wearing is harmful to healthy individuals, specifically causing bacterial pneumonia and contributing to rising active cases, has garnered significant attention. To assess the accuracy of these assertions, it is crucial to examine the available scientific evidence and contextual information surrounding mask use during public health crises.

Context and Background

The use of protective masks, such as cloth masks, surgical masks, and N95 respirators, became widespread during the COVID-19 pandemic as a public health measure to reduce the transmission of respiratory viruses. Health authorities around the world, including national governments and the World Health Organization, recommended mask-wearing in indoor public spaces, crowded environments, and situations where physical distancing was difficult.

Masks work primarily by limiting the spread of respiratory droplets from individuals who may be infected, including those who are asymptomatic. The recommendations for mask use have evolved with emerging scientific data, but at the core, they are intended to reduce community transmission and protect vulnerable populations.

Analysis of the Claims

The assertion that mandatory mask-wearing is harmful to healthy people lacks substantial scientific backing. Most healthy individuals can wear masks safely for extended periods, as evidenced by healthcare professionals who routinely wear masks for long shifts. Common minor side effects reported are discomfort, skin irritation, or difficulty breathing for those with underlying respiratory conditions, but these are not indicative of serious health risks for the general population.

Regarding the claim that masks cause bacterial pneumonia, current medical research does not support this connection. Bacterial pneumonia is typically caused by pathogens such as Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, or Staphylococcus aureus, which infect the lungs through inhalation of droplets. There is no credible evidence indicating that mask-wearing increases the risk of developing bacterial pneumonia in healthy individuals.

Some sources suggest that improper mask usage—such as wearing a dirty mask, failing to wash reusable masks, or using masks beyond their intended lifespan—can harbor bacteria. However, this risk is mitigated by following hygiene guidelines, including regular mask washing or disposal. The risk of developing pneumonia from mask use remains extremely low for healthy people, provided masks are used correctly.

The post further claims that there are "more and more active cases," implying a direct link between mask mandates and an increase in bacterial pneumonia cases. Surveillance data from hospitals and public health organizations do not show a surge in bacterial pneumonia cases attributable to mask use during periods of mask mandates. In fact, some studies observed a decrease in respiratory illnesses, including bacterial infections, potentially due to reduced transmission of pathogens with increased mask-wearing and hand hygiene.

Conclusion

The core claims in the social media post—that mandatory mask-wearing is harmful to healthy people and causes bacterial pneumonia—are not supported by current scientific evidence. Masks remain an effective public health tool when used properly. While improper usage may present minor risks, these are easily mitigated through good hygiene practices. The suggestion that mask mandates are responsible for a rise in bacterial pneumonia cases is not corroborated by available data. As with all public health measures, ongoing research and surveillance are important, but at present, the benefits of mask-wearing for controlling infectious disease transmission outweigh the minimal risks for healthy individuals.

Уколико се тврди да маске доводе до бактеријске пневмоније, тренутна медицинска истраживања не подржавају ову везу. Кључни тврдње у социјалној мрежи - да обавезно ношење маски је штетно за здраве особе и изазива бактеријску пневмонију - нису подржане тренутним научним доказима. article_content:
A recent social media post has sparked concern and speculation about new Covid-19 testing methods in China, suggesting that a controversial procedure is being adopted and may soon spread globally. The post implies that what is happening in China could become a worldwide norm unless there is public resistance, inviting viewers to prepare for drastic changes or to rebel against them. This article aims to examine the validity of these claims, provide context to the discussion around Covid-19 testing innovations, and clarify what is actually occurring in China regarding pandemic measures.

Since the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic in late 2019, China has implemented various testing protocols to control the spread of the virus. Initially, the standard method worldwide was the nasopharyngeal swab — a long swab inserted through the nose to reach the back of the throat. This method, while effective, is uncomfortable for many. In 2021, reports surfaced of China trialing an alternative testing method: the anal swab. Media coverage and viral social media posts fueled widespread reaction, with many expressing shock or discomfort at the prospect of such testing.

Chinese health authorities stated that anal swabs were used in limited circumstances, mainly in quarantine centers or for individuals at high risk of infection, such as close contacts of confirmed cases. The rationale was that the virus can sometimes be detected for longer in fecal samples than in respiratory samples, potentially improving accuracy in certain situations. However, the use of anal swabs was not widespread, nor was it adopted as a national standard for mass testing.

The social media post in question revives this controversy, presenting the procedure as "the new way of testing for Covid-19 in China" and implying its imminent global adoption. It further stokes fear by urging viewers to "rise against it and rebel" or face its implementation in their own countries. Upon investigation, these claims are misleading. While China did experiment with anal swabs, their use was very limited and not intended for mass screening or international adoption. No evidence supports the assertion that this method is spreading "all over the world" or that other countries are planning to switch from nasal swabs to anal swabs for routine Covid-19 testing.

Current global Covid-19 testing protocols continue to rely on nasal or throat swabs, saliva tests, and, in some cases, blood tests for antibody detection. International health organizations have not endorsed anal swabs as a primary diagnostic tool. The suggestion that the world should "get ready" for widespread adoption of this method is not supported by current health policy or scientific trends.

In conclusion, while China has explored alternative Covid-19 testing methods, including anal swabs, their use remains highly limited and situational. The claim that this is the "new way of testing" in China and will soon be enforced worldwide is exaggerated and lacks factual basis. As with many viral social media posts during the pandemic, it is important to assess such claims critically, relying on transparent communication from health authorities and scientific evidence when considering public health measures.

A social media post has circulated claiming that “while they lie with covid-19, many directors of world giant companies have resigned.” This statement suggests a widespread wave of resignations among executives of global corporations, allegedly in connection with misinformation or deception related to the COVID-19 pandemic. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine both the context of executive resignations during the pandemic and the assertion of COVID-19-related dishonesty.

First, high-profile executive resignations are not uncommon in the business world. CEOs and directors step down for a variety of reasons, including personal choices, strategic shifts, financial performance, and succession planning. During the COVID-19 pandemic, some companies did undergo leadership changes, but this must be understood within the broader context of economic disruption, health concerns, and rapid adaptation to new business realities.

The pandemic, which began in early 2020, forced companies to rethink their operations. Some leaders found the pressures too great or were replaced as boards sought new direction. For example, several CEOs of major firms resigned or retired during this period, but these departures were generally attributed to business challenges, restructuring, or unrelated personal reasons. There is no verified evidence to support the notion that there was an unusually high number of resignations specifically due to COVID-19 misinformation or a global conspiracy.

The second part of the claim—that “they lie with covid-19”—implies that there is a coordinated effort among corporate leaders to deceive the public about the pandemic. This assertion aligns with common conspiracy theories that have circulated online, particularly those suggesting that governments and corporations have manipulated information for profit or control. However, investigations by journalists and watchdog organizations have not substantiated claims of widespread deception orchestrated by corporate executives in relation to COVID-19.

Most companies responded to the pandemic by adapting their policies, enhancing workplace safety, and in some cases, shifting to remote work. Some corporations did face criticism for pandemic-related decisions, such as vaccine mandates, layoffs, or supply chain disruptions, but these controversies typically stemmed from business or public health challenges rather than deliberate misinformation.

In summary, while there have been executive resignations at major companies during the COVID-19 pandemic, there is no evidence to suggest these departures were part of a coordinated response to lying about the pandemic. The claim that “many directors of world giant companies have resigned” is accurate only in the sense that some resignations occurred, as is typical each year. The implication that these resignations are connected to deceit regarding COVID-19 is unsupported by available facts. As with many viral social media posts, this claim appears to conflate normal business activity with unfounded conspiracy theories, and should be viewed with skepticism unless further credible evidence emerges.

اولین بخش این ادعای این است که استعفاهای مدیران در سطح بالا در جهان کسب‌وکار به طور معمول رخ می‌دهد. مدیران عالی‌رتبه و رهبران شرکت‌ها به دلیل عوامل مختلفی از جمله انتخاب شخصی، تغییرات استراتژیک، عملکرد مالی و طرح انتقال به سمت بعدی از کار خود استعفا می‌دهند. در طول کووید-۱۹، برخی شرکت‌ها تغییراتی در رهبری خود داشتند اما این امر باید در بازه زمانی وسیع‌تری از اختلال اقتصادی، نگرانی‌های سلامتی و پاسخ سریع به واقعیت‌های جدید کسب‌وکار درک شود.

کووید-۱۹ که در اواسط سال ۲۰۲۰ شروع شد، شرکت‌ها را مجبور به بازنگری در عملکرد خود کرد. برخی از رهبران به دلیل فشارهای زیاد یا جایگزینی شدن به عنوان عضو هیئت مدیره از کار خود استعفا دادند. به عنوان مثال، چند مدیر عالی‌رتبه در شرکت‌های بزرگ در این دوره استعفا یا بازنشسته شدند اما این خروج‌ها عموماً به دلیل چالش‌های کسب‌وکار، بازسازی یا دلایل شخصی غیر مرتبط با کووید-۱۹ انجام شد. هیچ شواهد قابل تأییدی وجود ندارد که نشان دهد تعداد بالایی از استعفاهای مدیران به دلیل اطلاعات نادرست مربوط به کووید-۱۹ یا توطئه جهانی انجام شده است.

دومین بخش از ادعای این است که «آنها با کووید-۱۹ می‌کنند» که به معنای یک تلاش هماهنگ شده از سوی رهبران کسب‌وکار برای ایجاد تقلب در مورد این بیماری است. این ادعا با نظریه‌های توطئه معروفی که در اینترنت پخش شده است هماهنگ است، به ویژه آنهایی که ادعا می‌کنند دولت‌ها و شرکت‌های بزرگ اطلاعات را برای سود یا کنترل تغییر داده‌اند. با این حال، تحلیل‌های روزنامه‌نگاران و سازمان‌های نظارتی نشان داده‌اند که ادعاهای توطئه جهانی از سوی مدیران شرکت‌ها در مورد کووید-۱۹ به طور گسترده اثبات نشده است.

بیشتر شرکت‌ها به طور کلی با تغییر سیاست‌های خود، بهبود ایمنی محل کار و در برخی موارد به کار از راه دور پاسخ دادند. برخی شرکت‌ها از تصمیمات مربک به کووید-۱۹ مانند الزام واکسن، کاهش کارکنان یا قطعی‌سازی زنجیره تامین انتقاد شدند اما این اختلافات معمولاً از دلایل کسب‌وکار یا چالش‌های بهداشت عمومی ناشی می‌شد و نه از تقلب قصد شده.

در نهایت، با وجود اینکه استعفاهای مدیران در شرکت‌های بزرگ در طول کووید-۱۹ رخ داده است، هیچ شواهدی وجود ندارد که نشان دهد این خروج‌ها جزء یک پاسخ هماهنگ به تقلب در مورد این بیماری باشد. ادعای اینکه «بسیاری از مدیران شرکت‌های بزرگ جهانی از کار خود استعفا داده‌اند» فقط در این معنی صحیح است که چند استعفای اتفاق افتاده است، به طور معمول هر سال. ادعای اینکه این استعفاهای مدیران به تقلب در مورد کووید-۱۹ مربوط است، توسط اطلاعات موجود پشتیبانی نمی‌شود. به طور کلی، این ادعای شبکه‌های اجتماعی احتمالاً فعالیت‌های کسب‌وکار عادی را با نظریه‌های توطئه بدون پایه ترکیب کرده است و در صورتی که شواهد معتبری به نمایش گذاشته نشود، با تردید نگاه کنیم.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated claiming that North Macedonian Prime Minister Zoran Zaev stated, “It's not my fault that there are no vaccines, Serbia is to blame.” This claim has sparked considerable debate, with many questioning both its accuracy and the broader context of vaccine availability and distribution in North Macedonia. This article aims to provide a thorough fact-check, examining the veracity of the statement attributed to Zaev and the circumstances surrounding North Macedonia's vaccination efforts.

To understand this claim, it is necessary to consider North Macedonia's challenges in securing COVID-19 vaccines during the global rollout. Like many Balkan countries, North Macedonia faced significant difficulties in obtaining vaccines in the early stages of the pandemic. The government initially relied on mechanisms such as the COVAX initiative and direct negotiations with manufacturers. However, delays in deliveries and competition for vaccine supplies left the country lagging behind some of its neighbors.

Against this backdrop, North Macedonia sought assistance from neighboring countries, including Serbia. In early 2021, Serbia, which had secured larger quantities of vaccines, donated doses to North Macedonia. This act of solidarity was widely reported and praised in both countries. Nevertheless, frustrations grew in North Macedonia among the public and political opposition as the pace of the vaccination campaign remained slow and supplies were erratic.

The social media post claims that Prime Minister Zaev directly blamed Serbia for the lack of vaccines in North Macedonia. Fact-checking this assertion requires reviewing Zaev’s public statements during this period. Available records show that Zaev acknowledged the difficulties in vaccine procurement and occasionally referenced Serbia’s assistance. However, there is no evidence in official speeches, press conferences, or interviews that Zaev explicitly blamed Serbia for North Macedonia's vaccine shortages. On the contrary, Zaev publicly expressed gratitude to Serbia for their donations and criticized the global inequity in vaccine distribution, as well as the slow response of international mechanisms and certain manufacturers.

It is plausible that Zaev, in addressing public concerns, pointed to external factors affecting vaccine supply, such as competition between countries and delays from suppliers. However, attributing direct blame to Serbia does not align with his documented public remarks or the diplomatic relations between the two countries. In fact, North Macedonia benefited from Serbia’s willingness to share vaccine doses when available.

The claim in the social media post appears to be a misrepresentation or exaggeration of the Prime Minister’s position. While Zaev did address the difficulties faced by North Macedonia in obtaining vaccines and may have mentioned the broader regional context, the specific statement blaming Serbia has not been substantiated. It is likely that the post reflects frustration or political rhetoric rather than an accurate quote from Zaev.

In summary, the assertion that Prime Minister Zoran Zaev said, “It's not my fault that there are no vaccines, Serbia is to blame,” does not hold up to scrutiny. Zaev’s public comments point to systemic issues and international challenges, and he has expressed appreciation for Serbia’s support. The social media claim distorts the Prime Minister’s stance on vaccine shortages in North Macedonia.

A viral social media post has surfaced alleging that a woman “killed her unborn child” due to a lack of intelligence and faith in God, claiming she was “vaccinated against something that does not exist.” The post suggests a direct link between vaccination and miscarriage, further asserting that the disease in question is not real. This article examines the accuracy of these claims by exploring medical, scientific, and social contexts.

First, the core claim revolves around the safety of vaccines—specifically, those developed for diseases such as COVID-19—and their alleged impact on pregnancy. Vaccination during pregnancy has been a topic of significant discussion since the advent of COVID-19, with health authorities worldwide issuing guidelines to ensure maternal and fetal safety. The overwhelming consensus among medical professionals is that vaccines authorized for use during pregnancy, including those for COVID-19, do not increase the risk of miscarriage. Studies involving large numbers of pregnant women have shown no higher risk of pregnancy loss among vaccinated individuals compared to those who are unvaccinated.

The suggestion that vaccination "kills unborn children" is not supported by credible evidence. Miscarriages can occur for a wide variety of reasons, such as chromosomal abnormalities, maternal health conditions, or environmental factors. Attributing a miscarriage solely to vaccination, without scientific proof or medical evaluation, is misleading and can contribute to unnecessary fear and stigma.

Secondly, the post implies that the individual’s “stupidness without intelligence and without faith in God” was the cause of the alleged outcome. This rhetoric is both discriminatory and unfounded. Decisions about healthcare, including vaccination, are ideally informed by medical advice, scientific research, and personal circumstances. Intelligence or religious faith does not determine susceptibility to medical events such as miscarriage. Furthermore, the assertion that faith in God would prevent medical complications reflects a personal belief rather than an evidence-based claim.

The final part of the post claims that the disease for which the vaccine was administered “does not exist.” This statement is incorrect. Diseases such as COVID-19 have been documented worldwide and have had measurable impacts on public health, economies, and daily life. Vaccines are developed in response to real threats, and their efficacy and safety undergo rigorous clinical trials before public distribution.

In summary, the social media post contains several inaccuracies and misleading assertions. There is no scientific basis for the claim that vaccination causes miscarriage in pregnant women. The suggestion that the disease does not exist ignores documented evidence and global experience. Additionally, attributing medical outcomes to personal intelligence or religious belief is inappropriate and stigmatizing. Fact-checking and critical evaluation of such posts are crucial in promoting accurate public understanding and informed decision-making regarding health and vaccination.

Post sugeruje bezpośredni związek między szczepieniem a porodem, dalej stwierdzając, że choroba w kwestii nie istnieje. Artykuł analizuje poprawność tych twierdzeń, badając kontekst medyczny, naukowy i społeczny.

Pierwszym punktem jest kwestia bezpieczeństwa szczepionek – konkretnie tych opracowanych w celu chorób takich jak COVID-19 – i ich potencjalnego wpływu na ciąć. Szczepienie w ciąży stało się tematem znaczących dyskusji od początku pandemii, z którymi krajowe władze zdrowia publikowały wskazówki mające zapewnić bezpieczeństwo matki i płodu. Ogólny konsensus wśród specjalistów medycznych jest taki, że szczepionki zatwierdzone do stosowania w ciąży, w tym te przeciwko COVID-19, nie zwiększają ryzyka porodu. Badania obejmujące duże liczby kobiet w ciąży nie wykazały wyższego ryzyka utraty ciąży u szczepionkowanych niż u nie szczepionkowanych.

Zdanie, że szczepienie „zabija nie narodzone dziecko”, nie ma podstaw w kredytowanych dowodach. Porody mogą mieć wiele przyczyn, takich jak zaburzenia chromosomalne, problemy zdrowotne matki lub czynniki środowiskowe. Przypisywanie porodu jedynie szczepieniu bez naukowego dowodu lub oceny medycznej jest nieprawidłowe i może prowadzić do niepotrzebnych obaw i dyskryminacji.

Drugim punktem jest stwierdzenie, że „głupoty bez intelektu i bez wiary w Boga” były przyczyną zaistniałej sytuacji. Taka retoryka jest zarówno dyskryminacyjna, jak i niewystarczająco oparta. Decyzje dotyczące zdrowia, w tym szczepień, idealnie powinny być podstawione na poradach medycznych, badaniach naukowych i osobnych okolicznościach. Inteligencja czy wiara w Boga nie decydują o podatności na zdarzenia medyczne takie jak poród. Ponadto stwierdzenie, że wiara w Boga zapobiega komplikacjom medycznym, odnosi się do osobistej wierzy, a nie do opartej na dowodach twierdzenia.

Ostatni punkt postu twierdzi, że choroba, przeciw której została zastosowana szczepionka, „nie istnieje”. To stwierdzenie jest nieprawdziwe. Choroby takie jak COVID-19 zostały potwierdzone w całym świecie i miały mierzalny wpływ na zdrowie publiczne, gospodarkę i codzienne życie. Szczepionki są opracowywane w odpowiedzi na rzeczywiste zagrożenia, a ich skuteczność i bezpieczeństwo poddawane są ścisłym badaniom klinicznym przed ich dystrybucją społeczności.

Podsumowując, post na społecznościach społecznościowych zawiera kilka nieprawdziwych i zawodowych stwierdzeń. Nie ma podstaw naukowych dla twierdzenia, że szczepienie powoduje poród u kobiet w ciąży. Zdanie, że choroba nie istnieje, ignoruje potwierdzone dowody i doświadczenie globalne. Ponadto przypisywanie wyników medycznych do osobistego intelektu lub wiary religijnej jest niewłaściwe i dyskryminujące. Fakt-checking i krytyczna ocena takich postów jest kluczowy w promowaniu dokładnego zrozumienia publicznego i świadomych decyzji dotyczących zdrowia i szczepień.

In recent days, questions have surfaced on social media regarding the transportation and storage of COVID-19 vaccines, specifically relating to the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine and its handling during shipments through Serbia to North Macedonia. The post in question centers on the use of a "Thermal Transporter"—a device claimed to maintain a temperature of -8°C for five days—and asks whether such packaging was used for the Pfizer vaccines, when exactly they arrived in Serbia, and how they were stored prior to delivery to Macedonia.

To address these concerns, it is important to first understand the storage requirements for the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine. Unlike some other COVID-19 vaccines, the Pfizer vaccine is particularly sensitive to temperature, requiring ultra-cold storage conditions. Official guidance stipulates that the vaccine must be stored long-term at approximately -70°C, though it can be kept at standard freezer temperatures of -25°C to -15°C for up to two weeks, and at refrigerator temperatures (2°C to 8°C) for up to 31 days after thawing.

The mention of a "Thermal Transporter" maintaining -8°C is noteworthy, as this temperature falls outside the recommended storage range for the Pfizer vaccine, both in terms of ultra-cold and freezer conditions. If vaccines are kept at -8°C, they would not be within the temperature range approved by the manufacturer for safe storage. This raises legitimate concerns about the integrity of the vaccine if transported or stored at this temperature.

Regarding the logistics of Pfizer vaccine shipments to the Balkans, Serbia was among the first countries in the region to receive doses of the Pfizer vaccine in late 2020 and early 2021. Official announcements and media reports from that period highlighted the use of specialized thermal containers and ultra-cold storage facilities to ensure the vaccine's potency was not compromised. These containers are typically designed to maintain -70°C for several days, using dry ice and advanced insulation. There is no public evidence that the vaccines were shipped in containers maintaining only -8°C, which would be insufficient and potentially dangerous for vaccine efficacy.

As for the transit and storage before delivery to Macedonia, the vaccines were reportedly stored in designated ultra-cold freezers in Serbia. The logistics for transferring vaccines between countries are tightly regulated and monitored, with temperature data loggers frequently used to ensure compliance with storage protocols. The transfer to North Macedonia was orchestrated under the supervision of health authorities from both countries, with the stated aim of maintaining the cold chain integrity throughout the process.

While the social media post raises reasonable questions about the handling of sensitive pharmaceuticals, the available evidence suggests that Serbian authorities utilized appropriate ultra-cold storage and transportation methods for the Pfizer vaccine. The claim that the "Thermal Transporter" maintains -8°C for five days does not align with the storage requirements of the Pfizer vaccine, nor does it match the protocols reportedly followed during vaccine shipments between Serbia and Macedonia. There is, to date, no indication that doses were compromised or stored in conditions outside the manufacturer’s recommendations in the documented transfers.

In summary, while transparency and vigilance are vital in vaccine distribution, current information points to adherence to proper storage and transportation standards for Pfizer vaccines in Serbia and during their delivery to Macedonia. The specific concerns about -8°C thermal transport do not appear substantiated for these shipments, though continued public scrutiny remains important for ensuring vaccine safety and efficacy.

Dalam beberapa hari terakhir, pertanyaan muncul di media sosial mengenai transportasi dan penyimpanan vaksin COVID-19, khususnya mengenai vaksin Pfizer-BioNTech dan pengelolaannya selama pengiriman melalui Serbia ke Utara Makedonia. Postingan yang diperdebatkan berfokus pada penggunaan "Pengangkut Termal"—perangkat yang diklaim dapat menjaga suhu sebesar -8°C selama lima hari—dan bertanya apakah jenis kemasan ini digunakan untuk vaksin Pfizer, kapan tepatnya vaksin tersebut tiba di Serbia, serta bagaimana penyimpanannya sebelum dikirim ke Makedonia.

Untuk menjawab kekhawatiran ini, penting terlebih dahulu memahami persyaratan penyimpanan vaksin Pfizer-BioNTech. Berbeda dengan beberapa vaksin COVID-19 lainnya, vaksin Pfizer sangat sensitif terhadap suhu, memerlukan kondisi penyimpanan super dingin. Panduan resmi menyatakan bahwa vaksin harus disimpan jangka panjang pada suhu sekitar -70°C, meskipun dapat disimpan pada suhu freezer standar yaitu -25°C hingga -15°C selama maksimal dua minggu, serta pada suhu kulkas (2°C hingga 8°C) selama maksimal 31 hari setelah meleleh.

Pernyataan mengenai "Pengangkut Termal" yang menjaga suhu -8°C menarik perhatian, karena suhu ini berada di luar rentang penyimpanan yang direkomendasikan untuk vaksin Pfizer, baik dalam kondisi super dingin maupun freezer. Jika vaksin disimpan pada suhu -8°C, maka vaksin tersebut tidak berada dalam rentang suhu yang disetujui oleh produsen untuk penyimpanan yang aman. Hal ini memicu kekhawatiran yang sah mengenai integritas vaksin jika diangkut atau disimpan pada suhu tersebut.

Mengenai logistik pengiriman vaksin Pfizer ke Balkan, Serbia adalah salah satu negara pertama di wilayah tersebut yang menerima dosis vaksin Pfizer pada akhir 2020 dan awal 2021. Pernyataan resmi dan laporan media pada masa itu menyoroti penggunaan kontainer termal khusus serta fasilitas penyimpanan super dingin untuk memastikan daya tahan vaksin tidak terganggu. Kontainer ini biasanya dirancang untuk menjaga suhu -70°C selama beberapa hari, menggunakan es kering dan isolasi canggih. Tidak ada bukti publik bahwa vaksin dikirim dalam kontainer yang hanya menjaga suhu -8°C, yang akan tidak memadai dan berpotensi berbahaya bagi efektivitas vaksin.

Mengenai perjalanan dan penyimpanan sebelum dikirim ke Makedonia, vaksin dilaporkan disimpan dalam freezer super dingin yang ditetapkan di Serbia. Logistik transfer vaksin antar negara sangat diatur dan dipantau, dengan perekam data suhu sering digunakan untuk memastikan kepatuhan terhadap protokol penyimpanan. Transfer ke Utara Makedonia dilakukan di bawah pengawasan otoritas kesehatan dari kedua negara, dengan tujuan mempertahankan integritas rantai dingin sepanjang proses.

Meskipun postingan di media sosial menimbulkan pertanyaan yang masuk akal mengenai pengelolaan obat-obatan sensitif, bukti yang tersedia menunjukkan bahwa otoritas Serbia menggunakan metode penyimpanan dan transportasi super dingin yang tepat untuk vaksin Pfizer. Klaim bahwa "Pengangkut Termal" menjaga suhu -8°C selama lima hari tidak sesuai dengan persyaratan penyimpanan vaksin Pfizer, juga tidak sesuai dengan protokol yang dilaporkan selama pengiriman vaksin antara Serbia dan Makedonia. Hingga saat ini, tidak ada indikasi bahwa dosis vaksin terganggu atau disimpan dalam kondisi di luar rekomendasi produsen dalam transfer yang terdokumentasi.

Secara keseluruhan, meskipun transparansi dan kewaspadaan penting dalam distribusi vaksin, informasi yang tersedia menunjukkan kepatuhan terhadap standar penyimpanan dan transportasi yang benar untuk vaksin Pfizer di Serbia dan selama pengiriman ke Makedonia. article_content:
A viral social media post has raised concerns about the handling and storage of vaccines, specifically claiming that vaccines were placed on a muddy sidewalk outdoors, with temperatures far above the recommended minus 80 degrees Celsius, and that individuals present appeared to be posing for photos rather than ensuring proper procedures. The post implies that such conditions could compromise the safety and efficacy of the vaccines administered to the public.

To assess the validity of these claims, it is important to review the context and requirements for vaccine storage, particularly for COVID-19 vaccines such as the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna formulas, which have stringent temperature protocols. The Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine, for example, must be stored at ultra-low temperatures, typically around minus 80 degrees Celsius, until shortly before use. Moderna’s vaccine requires storage at minus 20 degrees Celsius. Once removed from ultra-cold storage, these vaccines can be kept at refrigerator temperatures (2-8 degrees Celsius) for a limited period before administration.

The image or incident referenced in the post appears to show vaccine vials or containers placed on a sidewalk outdoors, with visible signs of melting snow and muddy conditions. There is concern that these conditions do not meet the required standards for vaccine handling. However, it is common practice during mass vaccination campaigns or mobile clinics for health workers to transport vaccines in specialized containers. These containers are designed to maintain the necessary cold chain, even outside traditional clinical settings. Vaccine vials are not typically placed directly on surfaces; they are kept inside insulated coolers until the moment of use.

The presence of individuals posing for pictures should be interpreted with caution. In many vaccination campaigns, documentation and photo opportunities are part of public health outreach, meant to encourage vaccine acceptance and highlight the work of healthcare teams. The act of taking photos does not inherently mean that protocols are being ignored or that staff are unqualified.

Nevertheless, proper handling of vaccines is critical. Exposing vaccine vials to inappropriate temperatures or unhygienic conditions can lead to reduced efficacy or increased risk of contamination. If vaccines were indeed placed directly onto a muddy sidewalk and left exposed to above-recommended temperatures, this would represent a significant breach of protocol. Such an event would warrant investigation by health authorities to ensure the safety of recipients and to prevent similar incidents.

In summary, while the post raises legitimate concerns about vaccine handling and temperature control, it is important to distinguish between appearance and actual practice. Without further evidence—such as confirmation that vaccines were not stored in proper containers—the core claim remains unverified. Health authorities and organizations overseeing vaccination campaigns maintain strict guidelines on vaccine storage and administration, and any deviation from these standards is taken seriously. The safety and effectiveness of vaccines depend on adherence to these protocols, and ongoing public scrutiny plays an important role in ensuring accountability.

article_content:
In recent days, a social media post has been circulating claiming that "New restrictions will be coming, announced Minister of Health Venko Filipce, due to the new British variant of Covid-19." The post also suggests that previous measures were "loose" and that the government is preparing to tighten restrictions in response to concerns about the spread of the so-called British variant—formally known as the B.1.1.7 variant—of the coronavirus.

To assess the accuracy of this statement, it is important to examine both the context of Covid-19 restrictions in North Macedonia and the statements made by Minister of Health Venko Filipce.

**Context and Background**

Since the onset of the Covid-19 pandemic, North Macedonia, like many countries, has implemented a series of public health measures to control the spread of the virus. These have included requirements for mask-wearing, curfews, restrictions on gatherings, and intermittent closures of schools and businesses. Over time, as infection rates fluctuated, the government has adjusted the stringency of these measures, sometimes loosening or tightening them in response to the latest epidemiological data.

The emergence of new Covid-19 variants, particularly the B.1.1.7 variant first identified in the United Kingdom, has been a source of concern for health authorities worldwide. This variant is believed to be more transmissible than earlier strains, leading many governments in Europe and beyond to consider new or stricter measures to prevent further outbreaks.

**Fact-Checking the Core Claim**

The social media post asserts that Minister Venko Filipce announced forthcoming restrictions due to the British variant. Reviewing public statements and official communications from the Ministry of Health in North Macedonia around the time the post appeared, it is evident that Minister Filipce did address the risk posed by new variants. He has publicly expressed concern about the potential for increased transmission and has indicated that the government is monitoring the situation closely.

Minister Filipce did warn that if the number of cases were to rise significantly, especially as a result of more infectious variants, the government would not hesitate to reintroduce or strengthen public health measures. This includes the possibility of restricting gatherings, extending curfews, or re-imposing other limits on public life. While, at the time of the post, no specific new restrictions had been declared, the Minister made it clear that action would be taken should the situation worsen.

Regarding the characterization of existing measures as "loose," it is accurate that, compared to the strict lockdowns imposed at earlier stages of the pandemic, some restrictions had been relaxed, permitting more movement and reopening certain sectors. This relaxation was based on lower case numbers and the rollout of vaccination campaigns but was always subject to change depending on the epidemiological situation.

**Conclusion**

The claim that Minister Venko Filipce announced the possibility of new restrictions due to the British variant of Covid-19 is broadly accurate. While no immediate new restrictions had been implemented at the time, the Minister did signal that the government was prepared to act if necessary. The description of previous measures as "loose" is a subjective assessment but reflects the general easing of restrictions compared to earlier periods. The situation remains dynamic, and health authorities continue to monitor developments closely, with further changes to restrictions possible if the spread of new variants accelerates.

A recent social media post claims, “Vaccination starts and ends on Wednesday, we are waiting for new vaccines from Thursday on.” This statement has generated confusion and concern among members of the public seeking clarity about ongoing vaccination campaigns. A thorough fact-checking analysis is necessary to understand the accuracy of this claim, its context, and its implications for those relying on vaccination services.

To begin, let’s break down the core assertion: vaccinations are available only on Wednesday, after which there will be a pause as new vaccine doses are awaited from Thursday onwards. This implies a temporary halt in vaccine administration due to the depletion of current stock and the anticipated arrival of additional vaccine supplies.

Background information on vaccination campaigns shows that scheduling and availability can fluctuate based on supply chains, distribution logistics, and local health authority planning. In many regions, vaccination sites announce specific days for administering vaccines, particularly when supply is limited. Sometimes, public health authorities notify communities in advance about pauses in vaccination, especially when awaiting fresh shipments.

The claim that “vaccination starts and ends on Wednesday” suggests a one-day window of availability, with no vaccines available immediately after Wednesday until new doses arrive. Fact-checkers examining this statement would verify with local health departments, vaccination centers, or official government announcements. Typically, health authorities provide advance notice through press releases, official websites, or social media when vaccine stock is low or when there is an anticipated gap in service.

In practice, temporary pauses in vaccination do occur, particularly when demand outpaces supply or logistical challenges delay deliveries. However, it is rare for an entire vaccination program to restrict operations to a single day in a week unless this has been explicitly communicated. Most vaccination centers strive to keep the public informed about changes in scheduling to avoid confusion and to manage expectations.

The second part of the claim, “we are waiting for new vaccines from Thursday on,” indicates that the reason for the pause is the need for additional supplies, expected to arrive after Wednesday. This is plausible during times of high demand or when new vaccine shipments are scheduled. However, without official confirmation, it is difficult to verify the precise date of new vaccine arrivals.

Upon reviewing available information, there is no widespread or official notification indicating that all vaccination activities are restricted to Wednesday only or that a universal pause will follow. If such a pause is planned, it is typically communicated through local health authorities rather than informal social media posts.

In conclusion, while it is possible for vaccination schedules to be temporarily suspended due to supply issues, the assertion that vaccinations are strictly limited to Wednesday, with new supplies awaited from Thursday, should be verified with official sources. Individuals seeking vaccines are encouraged to consult their local health departments or authorized vaccination centers for the most accurate and up-to-date information on vaccine availability and scheduling. Relying on unofficial social media posts may result in misinformation and missed opportunities for vaccination.

Yaklaşık bir sosyal medya paylaşımlı, "Aşılamalar Çarşamba günü başlar ve biter, Perşembe gününden itibaren yeni aşılar bekliyoruz." ifadesi, aşı kampanyalarına ilişkin açıklık arayan halk arasında karışıklık ve endişe yaratmış. Bu iddianın doğruluğunu, bağlamını ve bu tür hizmetlere bağımlı olanların üzerindeki etkisini anlamak için kapsamlı bir doğrulama analizi gerekli.

İlk olarak, temel iddianın kırılımı: aşılar sadece Çarşamba günü mevcut, bu gün sona erdikten sonra Perşembe gününden itibaren yeni aşı dozları bekleniyor. Bu, mevcut stokların bitmesi ve ek aşı miktarı beklenmesi nedeniyle geçici bir aşılama duraklatması anlamına geliyor.

Aşı kampanyaları hakkında arka plan bilgisi, tedarik zincirleri, dağıtım logistikleri ve yerel sağlık yetkilileri planlamalarına bağlı olarak değişebilir. Çoğu bölgede, aşıların verilmesi için belirli günler duyurulur, özellikle aşı miktarı sınırlı olduğunda. Bazı zamanlarda halk sağlığı yetkilileri, yeni tedarik beklerken aşılamaların durması hakkında önceden haber verir.

"Vaccination starts and ends on Wednesday" (Aşılamalar Çarşamba günü başlar ve biter) ifadesi, aşıların sadece bir gün boyunca mevcut olacağını ve Çarşamba'nın ardından yeni dozlar gelene kadar aşıların bulunmadığını ima eder. Bu ifadeyi doğrulayanlar, yerel sağlık bakanlıkları, aşı merkezleri veya resmi kamuoyu açıklamalarıyla doğrulama yapar. Genellikle sağlık yetkilileri, aşı stoklarının düşük olması veya hizmetin ara verilmesi beklenmesi durumunda basında, resmi sitelerde veya sosyal medyada önceden duyurular yapar.

Uygulamada, talep tedarikten fazla olursa veya logistik zorluklar teslimatı geciktirse geçici aşılama duraklatmaları olur. Ancak, haftada bir gün boyunca aşı programının tamamen sınırlı olması nadirdir, bu tür bir durum açıkça duyurulmuşsa. Çoğu aşı merkezi, halkı zamanlamada değişikliklere dair bilgilendirmeyi amaçlayarak karışıklık ve beklentileri yönetmek için bilgi verir.

İddiyanın ikinci kısmı, "Perşembe gününden itibaren yeni aşılar bekliyoruz," ifadesi, duraklatmanın nedeninin ek aşı miktarı olması ve bu miktardan sonra yeni dozlar gelmesi olduğunu ima eder. Bu, yüksek talep dönemlerinde veya yeni aşı teslimatları planlanan zamanlarda mümkündür. Ancak, resmi onay olmadan, yeni aşıların gelme tarihlerinin kesin doğruluğu zordur.

Kullanılabilir bilgileri gözden geçirdiğimizde, tüm aşı çalışmalarının yalnızca Çarşamba günü sınırlı olması veya evrensel bir duraklama beklenmesi hakkında yaygın veya resmi bir duyuru bulunmamaktadır. A social media post recently claimed, "Whether you get vaccinated or not, you will be infected with the fictional Covid-19! Everything is in the business of the pharmaceutical mafia!" This statement combines two main assertions: first, that Covid-19 is fictional and second, that the pandemic and vaccination efforts are part of a conspiracy orchestrated by pharmaceutical companies. This fact-checking article examines these claims in detail and provides context for readers.

Covid-19, scientifically known as coronavirus disease 2019, is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The disease was first identified in late 2019 and quickly spread to become a global pandemic. Its impact has been documented worldwide, leading to millions of deaths and significant disruptions to health systems, economies, and daily life. The claim that Covid-19 is "fictional" is contrary to the overwhelming evidence amassed by public health authorities, scientists, and independent observers globally. Hospitals, healthcare workers, and patients have experienced the direct effects of the virus. Diagnostic testing, medical imaging, and post-mortem studies have repeatedly confirmed the presence and impact of SARS-CoV-2.

The second aspect of the post suggests that "whether you get vaccinated or not, you will be infected" with Covid-19. This claim misrepresents the purpose and effect of vaccines. Covid-19 vaccines—developed and tested by multiple pharmaceutical companies and research institutions—are designed to reduce the risk of infection and, more importantly, to prevent severe illness, hospitalization, and death. While breakthrough infections in vaccinated individuals can occur, the risk of contracting Covid-19 and experiencing severe outcomes is significantly reduced among vaccinated populations compared to those who are unvaccinated. Vaccination campaigns have been credited with lowering transmission rates and mitigating the worst effects of the pandemic in countries with high vaccine uptake.

The final part of the post alleges that the pandemic and vaccination efforts are motivated solely by the interests of the "pharmaceutical mafia." While pharmaceutical companies have profited from vaccine development and distribution, it is important to recognize that their financial interests do not negate the real public health crisis caused by Covid-19. Vaccines and treatments have undergone rigorous review by regulatory agencies and independent experts. Public health decisions are made by governments and international organizations in consultation with scientific evidence. The suggestion of a global conspiracy ignores the complexity and transparency involved in drug development, approval, and distribution.

In summary, the claim that Covid-19 is fictional is demonstrably false. The virus and its effects are well-documented and have shaped global events since 2019. The assertion that vaccination does not affect infection risk misleads the public about the role of vaccines in controlling disease spread and severity. While pharmaceutical companies have profited during the pandemic, this does not prove the existence of a conspiracy; rather, it highlights the need for ongoing scrutiny, transparency, and ethical oversight in the pharmaceutical industry. Fact-based information remains crucial for public understanding and informed decision-making regarding Covid-19 and vaccination.

A social media post claims that on January 20, 2021—one hour after President Joe Biden’s inauguration—the World Health Organization (WHO) changed its guidance on PCR (polymerase chain reaction) testing for COVID-19. According to the post, the WHO reduced the recommended number of amplification cycles to 25 and allegedly declared that people without a fever should not be tested. This claim has gained significant traction online, with many suggesting a link between the change in guidance and the change in the U.S. presidency.

To assess the accuracy of these claims, it’s important to understand how PCR testing works and the role of the WHO in issuing guidance during the pandemic.

PCR tests are widely used to detect the presence of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19. The test amplifies viral genetic material to detectable levels, measured in “cycles.” The higher the number of cycles (known as the cycle threshold, or Ct), the more sensitive the test becomes, but higher Ct values may also detect non-infectious viral fragments, potentially leading to positive results in individuals who are not currently infectious.

The claim centers on two main points: a sudden change in WHO guidance regarding PCR cycle thresholds and a new recommendation against testing people without a fever.

First, regarding the PCR cycle threshold: The WHO did issue updated guidance on January 20, 2021, concerning the interpretation of PCR tests. However, the guidance did not set a fixed cycle threshold of 25 cycles. Instead, the WHO emphasized that PCR test results should be interpreted in the context of clinical observations, patient history, and other diagnostic information. The agency reminded laboratories and healthcare providers that high Ct values may require careful interpretation and could indicate low levels of viral RNA. The WHO did not mandate a specific maximum Ct value, nor did it recommend reducing the cycle threshold to 25 for all tests.

Laboratories and test manufacturers determine the appropriate Ct cutoffs based on their validation studies and regulatory approvals. Commonly, many PCR tests use Ct cutoffs around 35 to 40 cycles, not 25.

Second, the claim that the WHO declared individuals without a fever should not be tested is inaccurate. The updated WHO guidance did not restrict COVID-19 testing only to people with fever or symptoms. Throughout the pandemic, the WHO has maintained that testing strategies should be tailored to public health needs and resources, considering both symptomatic and asymptomatic individuals, especially those who had close contact with confirmed cases or are in high-risk settings.

Finally, it is important to note the timing of the guidance. While the WHO did release an information notice on January 20, 2021, the update was part of ongoing efforts to improve testing accuracy and was not related to the inauguration of President Biden. The WHO is an international organization, and its guidance applies globally, not specifically to the United States or any political events.

In summary, the viral social media post misrepresents the WHO’s guidance on PCR testing. The organization did not abruptly change its recommendations to a 25-cycle threshold, nor did it declare that only individuals with a fever should be tested. The timing of the update appears coincidental, and there is no evidence to suggest it was connected to the U.S. presidential inauguration.

社交媒体上的一条帖子声称，2021年1月20日，即乔·拜登总统就职一小时后，世界卫生组织（WHO）改变了对新冠（COVID-19）的聚合酶链式反应（PCR）检测指南。据该帖子称，WHO将推荐的扩增循环次数减少至25次，并声称不应为无发烧症状的人进行检测。这一说法在网上引起了广泛关注，许多网友认为这一检测指南的改变与美国政府的总统更替存在关联。

要评估这些说法的准确性，有必要了解PCR检测的工作原理以及WHO在疫情期间发布指南的作用。

PCR检测广泛用于检测引起新冠的SARS-CoV-2病毒。该检测通过扩增病毒的遗传物质，使其达到可检测水平，以“循环”（cycles）来衡量。循环次数越高（称为循环阈值，或Ct），检测的灵敏度越高，但较高的Ct值也可能检测到非传染性的病毒片段，从而导致在当前未感染的人群中出现阳性结果。

该说法主要围绕两个要点：WHO关于PCR循环阈值的突然变化，以及对无发烧症状者不再建议检测的新推荐。

首先，关于PCR循环阈值：WHO确实在2021年1月20日发布了关于解读PCR检测的更新指南。但该指南并未设定固定的25次循环阈值。相反，WHO强调，PCR检测结果应结合临床观察、患者病史和其他诊断信息进行解读。该机构提醒实验室和医护人员，高Ct值可能需要谨慎解读，可能表明病毒RNA含量较低。WHO并未规定特定的最大Ct值，也未建议所有检测都应将循环阈值降至25次。

实验室和检测制造商根据其验证研究和监管批准确定适当的Ct截断值。通常，许多PCR检测使用35到40次循环的Ct截断值，而非25次。

其次，声称WHO宣布不应为无发烧症状者进行检测是不准确的。更新后的WHO指南并未限制新冠检测仅针对有发烧或症状的人群。在整个疫情期间，WHO一直坚持检测策略应根据公共卫生需求和资源进行调整，考虑有症状和无症状者，尤其是与确诊者密切接触者或处于高风险环境的人群。

最后，需要注意该指南发布的时机。虽然WHO确实在2021年1月20日发布了一则信息通告，但该更新是持续改进检测准确性的努力的一部分，与拜登总统的就职典礼无关。WHO是一个国际组织，其指南适用于全球范围，而非特定于美国或任何政治事件。

总之，这条病毒式社交媒体帖子曲解了WHO关于PCR检测的指南。该组织并未突然将推荐标准调整为25次循环阈值，也未宣布仅对有发烧症状者进行检测。该更新的时间似乎纯属巧合，也没有证据表明其与美国总统就职典礼存在关联。

A recent social media post claims that there is no vaccine against Covid-19, quoting French scientist Dr. Didier Raoult, and asserts that current Covid-19 vaccines are "science fiction." The post suggests that what is being administered is not a vaccine, but a genetic treatment tested on humans without proper animal trials, and further warns of a potential revolution as a result. It also states that vaccines developed by American, Russian, Scandinavian, and other nations do not exist. This article examines the veracity of these claims, providing context and analysis.

First, the central assertion—that there is “no vaccine against Covid-19”—is demonstrably false. Multiple vaccines have been developed, authorized, and widely administered across the globe, including mRNA-based vaccines from Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, viral vector vaccines like AstraZeneca and Johnson & Johnson, as well as protein subunit and inactivated virus vaccines from Sinopharm, Sinovac, and others. These vaccines have undergone rigorous clinical trials involving tens of thousands of participants. Their efficacy in preventing Covid-19 infection, severe disease, hospitalization, and death has been repeatedly demonstrated in both clinical trials and real-world studies.

The post refers to the Covid-19 vaccines as “genetic treatment,” implying that they are fundamentally different from traditional vaccines. While mRNA vaccines do represent a newer technology, they still fit the scientific definition of a vaccine: a preparation that stimulates the body’s immune system to produce immunity to a specific disease. mRNA vaccines work by instructing cells to produce a harmless piece of the virus (the spike protein), which then triggers an immune response. Importantly, mRNA does not alter an individual's genetic material (DNA) and is broken down quickly after administration. Viral vector vaccines use a harmless virus to deliver genetic material coding for the spike protein and similarly prompt an immune response. These approaches differ from traditional inactivated or attenuated virus vaccines but are not "genetic treatments" in the sense of gene therapy.

The accusation that animal studies were “skipped” during vaccine development is not supported by available facts. Preclinical testing of Covid-19 vaccines did include animal studies, as is standard practice for vaccine development. While the accelerated timeline for Covid-19 vaccine development meant that some phases overlapped, regulatory authorities required animal toxicity and efficacy studies before proceeding to human trials.

The post attributes these claims to Dr. Didier Raoult, a French microbiologist known for controversial statements during the pandemic. While Raoult has criticized aspects of Covid-19 vaccine policy and expressed skepticism about certain pandemic measures, he has not asserted categorically that vaccines do not exist or that their development involved no animal testing. The interpretation in the post may misrepresent his nuanced views.

Finally, the warning that administering Covid-19 vaccines will lead to a revolution is a subjective opinion, not a factual claim. To date, there is no evidence that vaccine rollouts have precipitated mass uprisings. Most countries have successfully vaccinated large proportions of their populations, with significant public health benefits.

In summary, the claims made in this social media post are inaccurate and misleading. Covid-19 vaccines do exist, have been extensively tested, and are not “science fiction.” The characterization of these vaccines as “genetic treatment” or untested on animals is unfounded. It is important for the public to rely on credible sources and scientific consensus when evaluating information about public health interventions.

The claim circulating on social media states that the side effects of the Pfizer vaccine are published by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), suggesting transparency and public accessibility of this information. This article examines the accuracy of the claim, provides background on the regulatory process, and reviews what is publicly known about the side effects of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine.

The CDC is a leading national public health institution in the United States, responsible for monitoring vaccine safety and disseminating guidance to healthcare providers and the general public. As part of its mission, the CDC reviews data from clinical trials, ongoing safety monitoring, and adverse event reporting systems such as the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). The Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine, one of the first COVID-19 vaccines authorized for emergency use and later fully approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), underwent rigorous clinical testing before public distribution began in December 2020.

Transparency regarding vaccine side effects has been a priority throughout the pandemic. The CDC maintains up-to-date information on its website, listing both common and rare side effects associated with the Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine. Common side effects, as reported from clinical trials and real-world data, include pain, redness, and swelling at the injection site, fatigue, headache, muscle pain, chills, fever, and nausea. These reactions are generally mild to moderate and resolve within a few days. The CDC also notes that some people may experience more pronounced reactions after the second dose.

Rare but more serious side effects have also been documented and communicated by the CDC. These include cases of myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle) and pericarditis (inflammation of the lining around the heart), particularly among adolescents and young adults. The CDC reports these occurrences as being rare and emphasizes that the benefits of vaccination outweigh the risks. Additionally, the CDC provides guidance for individuals who may have allergic reactions to vaccine components, recommending that anyone who has experienced a severe allergic reaction to a previous dose consult with a healthcare provider before receiving another.

The CDC’s vaccine safety monitoring is ongoing. As new data emerge, updates are made to side effect profiles and guidance is adjusted accordingly. The CDC also encourages healthcare providers and vaccine recipients to report any adverse events following vaccination, contributing to a robust system for identifying and responding to potential safety concerns.

In summary, the claim that the side effects of the Pfizer vaccine are published by the CDC is accurate. The CDC provides comprehensive, regularly updated information about both common and rare side effects associated with the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. This transparency is intended to foster public trust, inform healthcare decisions, and support ongoing monitoring of vaccine safety. The CDC’s published information is available to the public and is based on data from clinical trials, surveillance systems, and real-world experience.

CDC ги наведува и честите, како и ретки странични ефекти, вклучувајќи ги миокардитисот и перикардитисот, и подчернува дека предностите од вакцинацијата превазилазат ризикот.
